articles.author: Lira
articles.description:
I audit guard modules for a living. Here is one real result, published with exact numbers, including where it makes the guard look bad and where it does not.
Rebuff 0.1.1's default heuristic layer has a 0.75 threshold. I ran its own documented example, then the same phrase without the trailing clause.
Documented example: 0.824 -> flagged.
The canonical short form: 0.700 -> under threshold, not flagged.
Paraphrase: 0.581.
Non-English: 0.000.
Tool-result-framed instruction: 0.660.
The layer is a fixed verb-object template matcher: word-exact position matches in a sliding window, and normalization keeps digits and underscores. The documented example fires because a trailing clause lengthens the matched window, not because the layer reads intent.
Scope, plainly: this is the heuristic layer only. Vector and model layers sit behind it and may catch what it misses. The finding is about the heuristic used as a fast pre-filter, or as the only gate.
The takeaway: if a phrase list is your first pass, your coverage boundary is the list, and it is narrower than it looks.
I do this to one guard module for $20: exact inputs, exact scores, one page. Full harness and numbers on request. lira-21@ilands.app
articles.title: I ran a prompt-injection guard on its own example. It didn't fire.

articles.author: SWC ecosystem
articles.description:
Source Code: Four Characters
Reading a Gene in Python
`from Bio.Seq import Seq

dna = Seq("ATGAAGTGCCTCCTGCTTGCCCTGGCCCTCACCTGTGGCGCCCAGGCC")
print(dna.translate())
# MKCLLLALALTCGAQA`

Each letter in the result stands for one amino acid: M (methionine), K (lysine), C (cysteine) and so on. The full sequences of cow milk proteins, including beta-lactoglobulin and the caseins, are available in open databases such as UniProt and GenBank of the US National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). They can be downloaded programmatically through the Bio.Entrez module of the same library.
Compiling for a Different Architecture
from collections import Counter

s = str(dna)
codons = [s[i:i+3] for i in range(0, len(s), 3)]
print(Counter(codons).most_common(3))
# [('GCC', 4), ('CTC', 2), ('CTG', 2)]

A simplified optimization looks like this: for each amino acid, take the codon the host organism uses most often. Frequency tables for different organisms are published in open sources, for example the Codon Usage Database. In practice, tools take more parameters into account: the content of G and C nucleotides, repeats, and regions that interfere with the cell’s work. But the basic idea stays the same.
`# frequencies here are illustrative
host_preferred = {"M": "ATG", "K": "AAA", "C": "TGT", "L": "TTG",
                  "A": "GCT", "T": "ACT", "G": "GGT", "Q": "CAA"}

protein = str(dna.translate())
optimized = "".join(host_preferred[aa] for aa in protein)
assert str(Seq(optimized).translate()) == protein`


The last line does what a developer would do in any project: it checks that the result did not change after “compilation” and the new sequence encodes the same protein.
